opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think it's worth being a bit careful about what the claim actually is, because it's easy to state it in a way that sounds more mystical than it is.

The starting point is that neural networks are what statisticians call singular models. In a regular model, think of a classical statistical model like linear regression, each distinct setting of the parameters corresponds to a distinct function, and near the true parameter the loss landscape looks like a nice quadratic bowl. That's the world where a lot of classical intuitions come from: the Bayesian information criterion, counting parameters as a proxy for complexity, the Laplace approximation, and so on.

Neural networks aren't like that. There are huge sets of parameters that implement exactly the same function. You can permute neurons, rescale weights across a ReLU, have dead units whose outgoing weights don't matter, and so on. So the set of parameters that achieve low loss isn't a point, it's some extended geometric object, and crucially it's not smooth. It has self-intersections, cusps, places where different branches meet. Those non-smooth points are the singularities.

What Sumio Watanabe showed, in singular learning theory, is that in the Bayesian setting these singularities aren't a technical nuisance. They actually determine the behaviour of learning. The key quantity is the learning coefficient, sometimes called the real log canonical threshold, which is a measure of how degenerate the geometry is near a solution. More degenerate, more singular solutions have a lower learning coefficient, and that means they occupy relatively more volume in parameter space near low loss. So the posterior concentrates on them preferentially. In effect, the learning coefficient replaces the naive parameter count as the right notion of model complexity, and the posterior is trading off loss against this geometric complexity.

So when we say singularities govern learning, the first-order meaning is that the structure of the posterior, which solutions the model "prefers" given a certain amount of data, is controlled by the geometry of these singular points rather than just by how low the loss is.

Then there's a dynamical version of the claim, which is where it connects to training. As you see more data, the trade-off between loss and complexity shifts. Early on, simple, highly degenerate solutions win even if their loss is a bit worse. As data accumulates, it becomes worthwhile to move to a solution with lower loss but higher complexity. These transitions look like phase transitions in the posterior. And a hypothesis a lot of us have been working on is that something analogous happens during stochastic gradient descent: training isn't a smooth slide downhill but passes through a sequence of these singular regions, with relatively sharp transitions between them, and those transitions correspond to the model acquiring new structure or capabilities.

I want to be honest that the rigorous theorems are about Bayesian learning, and SGD is a different process. So part of the research program is empirical: we estimate local learning coefficients during training of real models, transformers learning in-context learning, toy models of superposition, and so on, and we look at whether changes in that geometric quantity line up with what we'd call developmental stages, where the model's internal computation qualitatively changes. And so far the evidence has been encouraging. You do see these stage-like changes, and they line up with interpretable changes in what the network is doing.

So the way I'd put it is: the singularities in the loss landscape are where the interesting structure lives, and if you want to understand what a network learns and in what order, you should be paying attention to that geometry, not just the value of the loss. And from a safety and interpretability perspective, that's appealing, because it suggests there's a principled way to detect when a model is reorganizing its internal structure during training, which is exactly the kind of thing you'd want to be able to monitor.

fable-5.1.text:
So the starting point is that when we talk about training a neural network, what we're really doing is picking a loss function over the parameters and then descending it, and the natural geometric object to look at is the set of parameters where that loss is minimized. For a generic smooth function you'd expect those minima to be isolated points, nice quadratic bowls, and that's the picture most of classical statistics is built on. But neural networks aren't like that. The map from parameters to the function the network computes is highly degenerate. You can permute neurons, you can rescale weights across a ReLU, you can have units that are simply switched off, and all of those give you the same function and so the same loss. So the minimum isn't a point, it's a complicated set, and at many places on that set the geometry is singular. The Hessian has lots of zero eigenvalues, and the loss near those points isn't quadratic at all, it's more like some higher-order polynomial that flattens out in certain directions.

Now, the claim that singularities govern training is really Watanabe's insight from singular learning theory. If you ask how much a region of parameter space contributes to the posterior, or equivalently how a learning process trades off fitting the data against the volume of parameters that achieve a given loss, the answer in the singular case is controlled by an invariant of the singularity called the real log canonical threshold, or what we tend to call the learning coefficient. It's a rational number, it's typically much smaller than half the number of parameters, and it tells you how fast the volume of low-loss parameters shrinks as you tighten the loss threshold. Points on the minimum set with a lower learning coefficient are, in a precise sense, more degenerate, more "flat," and they get a larger share of the posterior. So the geometry of the singularities, not just the loss value, determines which solutions are preferred.

Where it gets interesting for training specifically is that you can measure this quantity locally along a trajectory, and what you see is that it isn't constant. Stochastic gradient descent tends to find itself in the neighbourhood of singular regions for extended stretches, and then transition from one to another. When you track the local learning coefficient across training, those transitions show up as fairly sharp changes, and they line up with the model acquiring or reorganising some structure, like learning induction heads in a transformer or developing a new feature. So the picture I'd give is that the loss landscape is organised by a hierarchy of singularities, and the trajectory is a kind of sequence of visits to increasingly complex ones, with the learning coefficient being the thing that tells you what phase you're in. That's what I mean when I say the singularities govern the process. They're not an obstacle to the theory, they're the structure that explains it.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to clarify is what we mean by a singularity. A neural network has a space of parameters, and each point in that space specifies a function. But many different parameter settings can specify the same function. And the structure of that redundancy can change from one part of parameter space to another. You might, for example, have a neuron whose outgoing weight is zero, so changing its incoming weights does nothing to the output.

That gives you a geometry that’s much more complicated than an isolated minimum with a nice quadratic bowl around it. And that geometry matters because training doesn’t simply ask, ‘Where is the lowest loss?’ There’s also the question of how much parameter space is available at a given loss, and how the dynamics can move through it.

In singular learning theory, you can make aspects of that precise. There are quantities, particularly the learning coefficient, that measure an effective complexity associated with this geometry. They influence the balance between fitting the data and occupying a large volume of parameter space. So two solutions with similar training loss can have quite different statistical significance.

Now, I’d distinguish the mathematical results about Bayesian learning from the claim about the trajectory of stochastic gradient descent in a large neural network. The former are much better established. Understanding exactly how those results explain the dynamics of actual training is an ongoing research problem.

So when I say singularities govern training, I mean that this geometry is a fundamental part of the explanation for which solutions are accessible and favored, and potentially for transitions between different kinds of solutions. I wouldn’t mean that we already have a theorem that predicts every stage of a language model’s training.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the first thing to clarify is what we mean by a singularity. A neural network can have many different parameter settings that implement exactly the same function. So the space of parameters is not a clean space where every direction corresponds to a distinct change in what the network does. There are redundancies, and there are places where those redundancies become more pronounced. Those are the singularities we’re talking about.

Why should that matter for training? Because training doesn’t just select a function according to how well it fits the data. It takes place in this very large parameter space, and the geometry of that space affects which solutions are accessible and how much probability accumulates around them. Two solutions might fit the data equally well, but have very different amounts of parameter space surrounding them that also fit well.

Singular learning theory gives us tools for making that distinction precise. In particular, there’s an invariant called the learning coefficient that measures a kind of effective complexity near a solution. It can be very different from simply counting parameters.

Now, I would qualify the word ‘govern.’ The mathematical theory is strongest for Bayesian learning and its asymptotic behavior. Connecting that to the actual dynamics of stochastic gradient descent in a large neural network requires further work. But the central idea is that these singularities aren’t just mathematical defects you can ignore. They encode something about the structure of the functions the network can learn, and that structure can help explain why some solutions are favored over others.
